meaning: Draws a natural conclusion from facts or information already given, or restates them in other words. The negative is a partial denial.
connection: Verb / i-adjective plain form; na-adjective + な; noun + の／である + わけだ

senses.label: No wonder
senses.meaning: Once you hear the reason, the result suddenly makes sense: “no wonder ...”, “that's why ...”. Often paired with 「だから」 or 「道理で」. Unlike 「〜はずだ」, the fact is already in front of you; the speaker is accepting the reason.
senses.connection: Plain form + わけだ (na-adjective + な, noun + な／という); often with 「道理で」, 「だから」, or 「なるほど」
examples: Oh, you lived in Japan for three years? No wonder your Japanese is so good.
The window's open. No wonder it's so cold.
I see, so that's how it is.

senses.label: In other words
senses.meaning: Restates what was said, or works out a logical conclusion: “in other words”, “that means ...”. Often with 「つまり」 or 「すると」. Common in explanations and reports.
senses.connection: Plain form + わけだ／わけです (written: わけである); often with 「つまり」
examples: If you study two hours a day, that means you study fourteen hours a week.
So, in other words, our pay goes up starting next month.

senses.label: It's not that ...
senses.meaning: 「わけではない」 doesn't deny the fact itself. It denies the conclusion someone might draw from it: “it's not that ...”, “not entirely ...”. Usually followed by 「が」 or 「けど」 and the real situation. 「わけでもない」 is even softer.
senses.connection: Plain form + わけではない／わけじゃない／わけでもない
examples: It's not that I dislike meat. I just don't eat much of it.
It's not that I'm bad at cooking. I just don't have time.
It's not as if I understood all of it.

senses.label: And so
senses.meaning: 「というわけで」 and 「そういうわけで」 at the start of a sentence or paragraph sum up what came before and lead to the result: “so”, “and that's why ...”.
senses.connection: (という／そういう) わけで、+ result
examples: And so, tomorrow's game has been postponed.
That's why I've decided to move next month.

notes: 「わけだ」, 「わけではない」, 「わけがない」 and 「わけにはいかない」 differ by only a few kana but mean completely different things: 「行くわけではない」 = it's not that I'm going; 「行くわけがない」 = there's no way I'd go; 「行くわけにはいかない」 = I can't go. Mixing them up flips your meaning.

「わけだ」 is a conclusion the speaker has finally “got” because the fact is already in front of them; for a prediction about something not yet confirmed, use 「はずだ」: ✕ (when you haven't reached them yet) 「もう着いたわけだ」 → ○ 「もう着いたはずだ」.
After a superior explains a mistake, answering 「だから失敗したわけですね」 sounds like you are commenting on or probing them; to show understanding, 「そうだったんですね」 or 「承知しました」 is more appropriate.
After na-adjectives and nouns it cannot attach directly: ✕ 「静かわけだ」 → ○ 「静かなわけだ」; ✕ 「学生わけだ」 → ○ 「学生というわけだ」.

daily.title: Getting it after a friend explains
daily.description: Once a friend gives the reason, 「わけだ」 means “that explains it”.
daily.example: What, you didn't sleep last night? No wonder you're tired.

daily.title: Gently correcting a guess
daily.description: When someone misunderstands, 「わけじゃない」 says “that's not what it is”.
daily.example: I'm not angry. I'm just a bit tired.

daily.title: Working out expenses
daily.description: Doing the math with family and stating the result with 「わけだ」.
daily.example: If it's 5,000 yen a month, that means we pay 60,000 yen a year.

work.title: Wrapping up a discussion in a meeting
work.description: The chair closes the discussion and states the conclusion with 「というわけで」.
work.example: So, I'd like to move forward with this proposal.

work.title: Interpreting data in a report
work.description: Explaining what the numbers mean with 「わけです」.
work.example: In other words, sales fell 20% from the previous year.

etymology: わけ is written 「訳」. It is generally thought to come from the verb 「分く／分ける」, originally “to divide, to distinguish”. Its meaning later extended to “logic, reason, cause”. So 「わけ＋だ」 means “there's a reason for this; that's how it is”. This gave rise to the “naturally so” and “in other words” uses.
formation: 「わけだ」 = the noun 「わけ（訳）」 (reason, logic) + the copula 「だ」, literally “(this) is where the logic lies”. The preceding clause modifies 「わけ」 like any noun-modifying clause, describing what that logic is, so it takes the plain form, with 「な」 after na-adjectives and 「の／という」 after nouns. When the speaker learns the cause and it matches the result in front of them, you get “no wonder”; when they follow the logic through to an equivalent conclusion, you get “in other words”. In 「わけではない」, what is negated is the logic (the conclusion), not the fact itself, hence a partial denial. 「というわけで」 takes “that logic” as a cause and carries it into what follows, giving “and so, that's why”.

similar.title: 〜はずだ
similar.explanation: 「はずだ」 is an inference from evidence about something not yet confirmed; with 「わけだ」 the fact is already in front of you and the speaker accepts the logic behind it. 「彼は来るはずだ」 is a prediction; 「だから来なかったわけだ」 is a moment of realization.

similar.title: 〜わけではない
similar.explanation: Same origin: the negative of 「わけだ」. 「わけではない」 doesn't deny the fact itself, only the conclusion drawn from it: 「嫌いなわけではない」 = it's not that I dislike it (there's another reason).

similar.title: 〜わけがない
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「わけ」 + 「が」 + 「ない」, “there's no such logic” → “there's no way”. 「高いわけがない」 = it can't be expensive; 「高いわけではない」 = it's not (necessarily) expensive. The strength is completely different.

similar.title: 〜ということだ (hearsay / conclusion)
similar.explanation: Both can mean “in other words”. 「ということだ」 is more objective and bookish, and can also report hearsay (“I hear that ...”); 「わけだ」 carries a subjective “I see, naturally” tone and cannot report hearsay.

meaning: “Can't (do) ...” because of logic, responsibility, social obligation, or common sense. With the nai-form, it means “can't not ...”.
connection: Verb dictionary form + わけにはいかない; verb nai-form + わけにはいかない

senses.label: Can't (in good conscience)
senses.meaning: It's not that you're unable. Your principles, position, or the rules won't allow it: “can't really ...”, “it wouldn't be right to ...”. Mostly used to explain your own position. 「わけにもいかない」 means “can't very well ... either”.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + わけにはいかない／わけにもいかない (polite: わけにはいきません)
examples: I have an exam tomorrow, so I can't go out and have fun.
I drove here, so I can't drink.
It's my manager asking, so I can't very well say no.

senses.label: Can't not do
senses.meaning: A double negative: you're obliged to do it. “Can't not ...”, “have no choice but to ...”. Compared with 「なければならない」, it stresses pressure from relationships or your position, with a sense of resignation.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + ないわけにはいかない
examples: It's my friend's wedding, so I can't not go.
If my teacher asks me, I can't refuse.

notes: Dictionary form gives “can't do it”, ない form gives “can't not do it”; one kana flips the meaning: 「行くわけにはいかない」 = I can't go; 「行かないわけにはいかない」 = I have no choice but to go.
Only for things you are able to do but can't because of principle, duty or social obligation; for lack of ability use the potential form: ✕ (can't swim) 「泳ぐわけにはいかない」 → ○ 「泳げない」.

When declining a client or superior, 「お受けするわけにはいきません」 sounds like a hard, principled refusal; in business, add a cushion and use humble language: 「大変申し訳ございませんが、お受けするわけにはまいりません」, or switch to 「〜いたしかねます」.
Don't confuse it with 「わけがない」: 「彼が行くわけがない」 = there's no way he'd go (inference); 「私は行くわけにはいかない」 = I can't go (a constraint on my own action).

daily.title: Declining an expensive gift
daily.description: Politely saying you can't accept something costly.
daily.example: I couldn't possibly accept something so expensive.

daily.title: Turning down a drink at dinner
daily.description: Explaining you can't drink because you're driving.
daily.example: I'm driving today, so I really can't drink.

daily.title: Going out of obligation
daily.description: When you don't really want to go but feel you must.
daily.example: It's a family gathering, so I can't skip it.

work.title: Explaining why you can't take a day off
work.description: Telling a coworker you have important work.
work.example: I've got an important meeting tomorrow, so I can't take the day off.

work.title: Seeing a job through
work.description: At a critical stage, saying you won't give up.
work.example: We've come this far. We can't give up now.

etymology: わけ（訳） originally means “reason, logic”. 「いかない」, the negative of いく（行く）, can mean “doesn't work out”, as in 「うまくいかない」. Together they literally mean “it doesn't work by reason”, that is, “you can't reasonably do that”. 「は」 strengthens the negative.
formation: 「わけにはいかない」 = 「わけ」 (reason, principle) + 「に」 (destination) + 「は」 (contrastive emphasis) + 「いかない」 (negative of 「行く」: doesn't go). Literally “you can't get through along that line of reasoning”, i.e. by principle, obligation or social convention, “that road is closed”. Because the obstacle is principle and social constraint rather than ability, it means “(could do it, but) can't”, never “don't know how / am unable to”. Put the ない form in front and it becomes “not doing it won't do” → “can't not do it”. The 「は」 is emphatic and is often dropped in speech: 「わけにいかない」; the formal version replaces 「いく」 with the humble 「まいる」: 「わけにはまいりません」.

similar.title: 〜ないわけにはいかない
similar.explanation: Same origin: with the ない form in front it means “can't not ... / have to ...”. 「休むわけにはいかない」 = I can't take the day off; 「休まないわけにはいかない」 = I have no choice but to take it. Check whether what precedes is affirmative or negative.

similar.title: 〜ざるを得ない
similar.explanation: Close in meaning to 「ないわけにはいかない」: both mean “have no choice but to”. 「ざるを得ない」 is more literary and stresses “no other option, so be it”; 「ないわけにはいかない」 stresses “it wouldn't be right, given duty or social obligation”.

similar.title: 〜なければならない
similar.explanation: Also “must”, but it merely states an obligation or rule objectively; 「ないわけにはいかない」 carries the nuance “I'd rather not, but I can't get out of it”: 「招待されたから、行かないわけにはいかない」.

similar.title: 〜わけがない
similar.explanation: Same origin but different meaning: 「わけがない」 is the inference “impossible”, 「わけにはいかない」 is “can't do it” as a constraint on action. 「彼が来るわけがない」 = there's no way he'll come; 「今帰るわけにはいかない」 = I can't leave now.

meaning: The subject makes a decision of their own free will. 「ことにしている」 is a rule you've set for yourself. It can also mean “treat it as ...”.
connection: Verb dictionary form / nai-form / ta-form + ことにする (ことにした／ことにしている)

senses.label: Deciding to
senses.meaning: The speaker (subject) decides something by choice: “decide to ...”. 「ことにした」, a decision already made, is the most common. 「ことにする」 is a decision made on the spot. Use the nai-form to decide not to do something.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form / nai-form + ことにする／ことにした
examples: I've decided to go jogging every morning starting next month.
After thinking it over, I decided to take on that job.
I'm going to quit smoking for good.

senses.label: A habit you keep
senses.meaning: 「ことにしている」 is a habit or personal rule based on your own decision: “I make it a rule to ...”.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form / nai-form + ことにしている
examples: For my health, I make it a rule not to drink coffee at night.
I make a point of getting up at seven every morning.

senses.label: Treat it as
senses.meaning: After the ta-form, it means treating the actual situation as if it were something else: “let's pretend ...”. Common phrases: 「聞かなかったことにする」 and 「なかったことにする」.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form / なかった + ことにする
examples: Let's pretend I didn't hear that.
Please consider that promise as never having been made.

notes: 「ことにする」 stresses “I decided this myself”, while 「ことになる」 sounds like “it just got settled”. Telling your company 「退職することにしました」 sounds unilateral and blunt; 「退職することになりました」 is the softer, usual way to put it.
Don't add 「こと」 when choosing a noun: ✕ 「私はコーヒーのことにします」 → ○ 「私はコーヒーにします」.
「〜ことにする」 (decide to) and 「〜たことにする」 (let's say that ...) differ only in the た form but mean completely different things: 「行くことにする」 = I decide to go; 「行ったことにする」 = let's say I went (though I didn't).
「ことにしている」 is a habit you have set for yourself and keep; it can't describe a one-off: ✕ 「昨日は早く寝ることにしている」 → ○ 「昨日は早く寝ることにした」.

daily.title: Announcing a decision to a friend
daily.description: Sharing a big decision you just made.
daily.example: I've decided to study abroad in Japan next year.

daily.title: Describing your habits
daily.description: Explaining a personal rule when talking about health.
daily.example: I make it a rule not to eat anything after 9 p.m.

daily.title: Keeping a friend's secret
daily.description: When a friend lets something slip, saying you'll act like you didn't hear.
daily.example: Don't worry, I'll pretend I didn't hear that.

work.title: Informing a client of a decision
work.description: Explaining your company's own decision in business, with humble 「いたしました」.
work.example: We have decided not to participate this time.

work.title: A student explaining a study plan
work.description: Telling a teacher about a study rule you've set.
work.example: I make a point of memorizing 20 words every day.

etymology: こと（事） is a formal noun that turns the preceding action into a noun. 「に」 marks the result of a choice, and 「する」 means the subject consciously does it. Literally, “to make (something) your choice”, which is why it stresses an active decision. By contrast, 「なる」 expresses natural change, giving 「ことになる」.
formation: 「ことにする」 = the formal noun 「こと」 + the case particle 「に」 + the verb 「する」. 「Aにする」 originally means “settle on A, choose A” (「コーヒーにする」); an action can't stand directly before 「に」, so 「こと」 first turns it into “a matter”, giving “fix the matter of doing X” → “decide to do X”. The predicate 「する」 is an active verb, so the decision is in the subject's own hands, which is exactly the opposite of 「ことになる」 with 「なる」 (happen naturally). 「ことにした」 reports the decision itself; 「ことにしている」 is the state of keeping to a decision, i.e. a personal habit. With a た form in front, it “sets” a past event as fact → “let's say that ...”.

similar.title: 〜ことになる
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「する」 means you decide it yourself, 「なる」 means it was decided by others, a rule or circumstances (or you deliberately don't foreground yourself). 「結婚することにしました」 stresses your own resolve; 「結婚することになりました」 sounds natural and modest.

similar.title: 〜つもりだ
similar.explanation: 「つもり」 is an intention in your mind, not necessarily firmly decided; 「ことにする」 is a decision reached after consideration. 「行くつもりだ」 = I intend to go; 「行くことにした」 = I've decided (after thinking) to go.

similar.title: 〜にする (decide / choose)
similar.explanation: Same origin: before a noun, use 「にする」 directly: 「コーヒーにする」 (I'll have coffee); before an action you need 「こと」 to turn it into a noun: 「コーヒーを飲むことにする」.

similar.title: 〜ことにしている
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「ことにしている」 is the state of keeping to a decision once made, a personal habit: 「毎朝走ることにしている」; 「ことにした」 only reports the moment of deciding.

meaning: A decision or arrangement made outside your own will. 「ことになっている」 expresses rules and set plans. It can also show a calculated result.
connection: Verb dictionary form / nai-form + ことになる (ことになった／ことになっている)

senses.label: It's been decided
senses.meaning: The decision was made by a company, school, other people, or circumstances, not actively by the speaker: “it's been decided that ...”. Even for your own decisions, 「ことになりました」 sounds modest and objective.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form / nai-form + ことになる／ことになった
examples: I'll be working at the Tokyo head office starting next year.
It's been decided that the meeting will be canceled.

senses.label: Rules and set plans
senses.meaning: 「ことになっている」 expresses rules, laws, customs, or a set schedule: “you're supposed to ...”, “it's scheduled that ...”.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form / nai-form + ことになっている
examples: In this dorm, you're supposed to be back by 10 p.m.
Phones are to be turned off during class.

senses.label: That means / will end up
senses.meaning: A result worked out by logic or calculation: “that means ...”, “you'll end up ...”. Often used to warn about consequences.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + ことになる (often with 「〜と」 or 「このままだと」)
examples: If you spend 1,000 yen a day, that's 30,000 yen a month.
At this rate, you're going to miss the deadline.

notes: 「ことになる」 means “it was settled (by others or circumstances)”, 「ことにする」 means “I decided”. Even when it was your own decision, 「ことになりました」 is a common modest way to put it in formal settings, but using it for your own mistake sounds like passing the blame.
For changes in ability or habit use 「ようになる」, not 「ことになる」: ✕ 「日本語が話せることになった」 → ○ 「日本語が話せるようになった」.
Company rules and customs take 「ことになっている」; don't say 「ことにしている」, which is a personal habit: ✕ 「この会社では9時に出社することにしている」 → ○ 「9時に出社することになっている」.
In 「大変なことになった」 and 「困ったことになる」, 「こと」 means “situation” and is preceded by an adjective; this is not the “settled decision” grammar point.

daily.title: Telling a friend you're moving
daily.description: For outside reasons like a parent's job transfer, 「ことになった」 sounds natural.
daily.example: Because of my dad's job, we're moving to Osaka.

daily.title: Explaining apartment rules
daily.description: Telling a new roommate the house rules.
daily.example: Garbage is supposed to go out on Tuesdays.

daily.title: Warning a friend of the consequences
daily.description: When a friend wants to quit, pointing out what it would mean.
daily.example: If you quit now, all your hard work will have been for nothing.

work.title: Announcing a transfer
work.description: Formally announcing your transfer at a morning meeting or by email.
work.example: I will be transferring to the Osaka branch in April.

work.title: Announcing a meeting date
work.description: Telling coworkers about a schedule that's been set.
work.example: The meeting has been scheduled for next Monday.

etymology: こと（事） is a formal noun; 「に」 marks the result of a change; 「なる」 means “to come about, to become”. Literally, “things have come to be ...”. Because 「なる」 doesn't highlight who acted, it presents a decision as formed outside the speaker's will. Japanese speakers also use it to sound modest and avoid seeming self-assertive.
formation: 「ことになる」 = the formal noun 「こと」 + the case particle 「に」 (result of a change) + the verb 「なる」 (become naturally). 「Aになる」 means “turn into A” and needs no one's will; put an action inside 「こと」 and it becomes “the matter of doing X has become settled”. So the one who decides is not the speaker but the company, the other party or circumstances, or the speaker deliberately hides themselves (modest, non-assertive). The state of having been settled and still holding, 「ことになっている」, is a rule, custom or schedule. With quantities and logic, “by calculation it comes to ...” → “that amounts to / in other words”.

similar.title: 〜ことにする
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「ことにする」 is a decision made by the speaker; 「ことになる」 is the result decided by others, an organization or circumstances, with the subject's will not evident. 「引っ越すことにした」 = I decided to move; 「引っ越すことになった」 = I'm moving (because of a transfer, etc.).

similar.title: 〜ことになっている
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「ことになっている」 is a rule, plan or custom that has been set and remains in force: 「ここではタバコを吸わないことになっている」; 「ことになった」 only reports the change of “it's been settled”.

similar.title: 〜ようになる
similar.explanation: The two are often compared: 「ようになる」 is a gradual change in ability, habit or state: 「話せるようになった」; 「ことになる」 is the result of a decision or arrangement: 「大阪に転勤することになった」.

similar.title: 〜わけだ
similar.explanation: Close in the calculation use: 「つまり月6万円払うことになる」 and 「払うわけだ」 are both possible. 「ことになる」 says objectively “the result will be ...”, while 「わけだ」 carries a sense of “I see, so that's how it works out”.

meaning: Expresses cause, means, the doer in passive sentences, and “varies depending on ...”. 「によると」 gives a source of information.
connection: Noun + によって／により／による + noun／によっては／によると・によれば

senses.label: Cause: due to
senses.meaning: States the cause of accidents, disasters, and so on objectively: “due to ...”, “because of ...”. Neutral in tone, common in news and notices. Not used as the reason for personal requests or commands.
senses.connection: Noun + によって／により (more formal)／による + noun
examples: The damage from the earthquake was greater than expected.
Trains have stopped due to heavy rain.

senses.label: Means: through
senses.meaning: The means or method by which something is achieved: “through ...”, “by means of ...”. More formal than the particle 「で」.
senses.connection: Noun + によって／により
examples: She achieved her dream through hard work.
Through the internet, we can get information from all over the world.

senses.label: Passive: by
senses.meaning: In passive sentences, it marks who created, invented, or discovered something: “(written / invented) by ...”. These sentences use 「によって」, not 「に」.
senses.connection: Noun (person) + によって + passive verb (書かれる, 発明される, etc.)
examples: This novel was written by Natsume Soseki.
The telephone was invented by Bell.

senses.label: Varies by
senses.meaning: Followed by 「違う」, 「異なる」, or 「さまざまだ」, it means things differ depending on the case. 「によっては」 means “depending on ..., some may ...”.
senses.connection: Noun + によって違う／異なる; noun + によっては
examples: Ways of thinking differ from person to person.
Depending on the situation, the game may be canceled.

senses.label: According to
senses.meaning: 「によると」 and 「によれば」 give a source of information: “according to ...”. The sentence often ends with 「そうだ」 or 「らしい」.
senses.connection: Noun (source) + によると／によれば
examples: According to the weather forecast, it's going to snow tomorrow.
According to the news, train fares are going up next month.

notes: The source of information (“according to ...”) takes 「によると／によれば」, not 「によって」: ✕ 「天気予報によって、明日は雨だそうだ」 → ○ 「天気予報によると、明日は雨だそうだ」.

The agent of a passive is normally marked with 「に」; 「によって」 is used only with verbs of creating (create, invent, discover, build) or in formal style: ✕ 「私は先生によって褒められた」 → ○ 「先生に褒められた」; ○ 「この寺は聖徳太子によって建てられた」.
「人によって」 = depending on the person (everyone differs); 「人によっては」 = some people will ... (only some): 「人によっては辛すぎると感じる」. Adding or omitting 「は」 changes the meaning.
The cause and means uses are bookish; in everyday speech 「〜で」 is more natural: 「病気で休んだ」. Saying 「病気によって休んだ」 in conversation sounds stiff.

daily.title: Chatting about regional customs
daily.description: Using 「によって違う」 to compare different places.
daily.example: Apparently New Year's dishes are different depending on the region.

daily.title: Passing on the weather forecast
daily.description: Telling family about the weather before going out.
daily.example: According to the forecast, it's going to rain from the afternoon.

daily.title: A temple tour
daily.description: A guide explains who built the building.
daily.example: This temple was built 400 years ago by a famous carpenter.

work.title: A station announcement about delays
work.description: Public announcements state causes objectively, often with 「により」.
work.example: Due to a passenger accident, trains are running behind schedule.

work.title: Explaining pricing to a customer
work.description: Explaining that prices change depending on conditions.
work.example: Fees vary depending on how long you use the service.

etymology: よる is written 「因る・依る・拠る・由る」, originally meaning “to rely on, to depend on, to be based on”. The old form 「によりて」 underwent a sound change to the small っ, becoming modern 「によって」. The stem form 「により」 kept its connective use and sounds more literary. Each kanji has a different focus: 因る = cause, 依る = means, 拠る = basis, 由る = origin.
formation: 「によって」 = the case particle 「に」 (the thing relied on) + the て form of the verb 「よる」 (因る・依る: depend on, rely on, be determined by). The core meaning is “relying on A ...”, and it branches into several uses depending on what is relied on: a tool or method = means; some cause = because of; the hands through which something comes into being = the agent of a passive; a result determined by A = varies with A. Since 「よる」 is a verb, it also appears as the continuative 「により」, the attributive 「による＋noun」, and the conditional 「によれば」 (going by ... → according to), each with its own function.

similar.title: 〜によると・〜によれば
similar.explanation: Same origin: the conditional of 「よる」, used only for the source of information, “according to ...”, often with 「そうだ」 or 「らしい」 at the end: 「ニュースによると、事故があったらしい」. 「によって」 has no such use.

similar.title: 〜によっては
similar.explanation: Same origin: with 「は」 it means “depending on the case, there are times when ...”, speaking of only some cases: 「人によっては」 = some people; 「人によって」 = it varies from person to person.

similar.title: 〜で (means / method)
similar.explanation: Both can express means or cause. 「で」 is the ordinary everyday form: 「バスで行く」, 「病気で休む」; 「によって」 is more bookish and formal, common in news, reports and explanatory writing.

similar.title: 〜に応じて
similar.explanation: Close in meaning to “varies by ...”. 「によって」 just says “differs according to A”; 「に応じて」 stresses “adjusting accordingly to the situation of A”: 「収入に応じて税金が変わる」.

meaning: Marks the topic of talking, thinking, researching, or explaining: “about ...”, “concerning ...”.
connection: Noun + について／については／についても／についての + noun (formal: につきまして)

senses.label: About (a topic)
senses.meaning: What you speak, write, think, or research about: “about ...”, “on ...”. Usually followed by verbs like 「話す・説明する・調べる・考える・聞く」. Adding 「は」 raises the topic or shows contrast.
senses.connection: Noun + について／については／についても
examples: I'm researching Japanese history.
I'd like to hear everyone's opinion on this issue.
I'll explain this point later.

senses.label: About ... (before a noun)
senses.meaning: Before a noun, use 「についての」: “a ... about ...”.
senses.connection: Noun + についての + noun
examples: I read a book about the environment.
I'm going to give a presentation on Japanese culture.

senses.label: Formal version
senses.meaning: In business, speeches, and other formal settings, 「につきまして」 is more polite than 「について」.
senses.connection: Noun + につきまして(は)
examples: Our representative will explain the details.
Please find our response to your inquiry below.

notes: 「について」 marks the content of what is discussed or thought about, not the target of an action or attitude: ✕ 「お客様について丁寧に対応する」 → ○ 「お客様に対して丁寧に対応する」.
Modifying a noun requires 「の」: ✕ 「日本について本」 → ○ 「日本についての本」 (or 「日本に関する本」).

In meetings and emails 「〜につきまして」 sounds polite: 「本件につきまして、ご説明いたします」. But a bare 「〜につき」 in notices often means “because of” or “per”: 「工事中につき通行止め」 = closed to traffic due to construction; don't misread it as “about”.

etymology: It comes from the verb 「就く（つく）」, originally meaning "to attach to, to approach, to follow". The old form 「に就きて」 became 「に就いて」 through i-onbin and was then written in kana as 「について」, meaning "attaching to ... (to talk)", i.e. "around ..., about ...". The continuative 「につき」 still appears in written language as 「〜につき」 (concerning / due to / per ...).
formation: 「について」 = the case particle 「に」 (object) + the て form 「ついて」 of the verb 「つく」 (就く・付く: stay close to, follow). Literally “stick close to A” while speaking or thinking, hence “centering on the topic A” → “about”. Because it means unfolding something while staying close to the topic, it is mostly followed by verbs of speech and thought such as 「話す・考える・調べる・説明する」, and not by attitudes or actions directed at a person. Its verbal nature survives in its other forms: 「についての＋noun」 modifies a noun, 「につき」 is a written continuative, and 「につきまして」 is the polite form.

similar.title: 〜に関して・〜に関する
similar.explanation: Nearly identical in meaning. 「に関して」 is more bookish and formal, used in official documents and reports; 「について」 is common in both everyday and spoken use. Before a noun, 「に関する＋noun」 is more concise and formal than 「についての＋noun」.

similar.title: 〜をめぐって
similar.explanation: Also “centering on ...”, but for a topic of dispute or opposition among several parties, followed by 「議論する」, 「争う」, 「対立する」; for a plain topic or content use 「について」: 「遺産をめぐって争う」.

similar.title: 〜に対して
similar.explanation: 「について」 marks the content being discussed; 「に対して」 marks the target an action or attitude is directed at: 「日本について話す」 = talk about Japan; 「客に対して丁寧に話す」 = speak politely to a customer.

meaning: Marks the target of an action, attitude, or feeling. It can also contrast two things or express a ratio (“per ...”).
connection: Noun + に対して／に対し／に対する + noun; contrast: plain form + の + に対して

senses.label: Toward (a target)
senses.meaning: The target an attitude, feeling, or action is aimed at: “toward ...”, “to ...”, “against ...”. Often followed by 「反対する・抗議する・親切だ・厳しい」. Before a noun, use 「に対する」.
senses.connection: Noun + に対して／に対しては／に対する + noun
examples: The teacher is very kind to the students.
Many people opposed that opinion.
Please be careful about how you speak to customers.

senses.label: In contrast to
senses.meaning: Puts two things side by side to contrast them: “whereas ...”, “in contrast to ...”. Add 「の」 after a clause. In writing, the stem form 「に対し」 is common.
senses.connection: Plain form (na-adjective / noun + な) + のに対して／のに対し
examples: My older brother is outgoing, whereas my younger brother is quiet.
While the urban population is growing, the rural population is shrinking.

senses.label: Per (ratio)
senses.meaning: Expresses a ratio: “per ...”, “for every ...”.
senses.connection: Quantity + に対して
examples: There is one teacher for every 20 students.
Out of 100 applicants, only five passed.

notes: 「に対して」 is followed by an attitude or action toward the other party; for “for / to (someone), it's difficult / important” use 「にとって」: ✕ 「私に対してこの仕事は難しい」 → ○ 「私にとってこの仕事は難しい」.
For a topic of discussion use 「について」, not 「に対して」: ✕ 「日本文化に対して研究する」 → ○ 「日本文化について研究する」.
In the contrast use, a clause needs 「の」 first: ✕ 「兄は背が高いに対して」 → ○ 「兄は背が高いのに対して、弟は低い」.

etymology: 「対する（たいする）」 is a suru-verb formed from the Sino-Japanese element 「対」 (on'yomi たい, "facing, opposite") plus する, originally meaning "to face, to be opposite, to oppose". に marks the target, and the te-form links to the following clause. The suspended form 「に対し」 and the attributive form 「に対する」 both come from the conjugation of this suru-verb and have the written flavor of the kanbun-reading style.
formation: 「に対して」 = the case particle 「に」 (direction, target) + the て form of the Sino-Japanese verb 「対する」 (face, be opposite). The core image is “facing A”: an action or feeling faces someone, which makes them its target (「先生に対して失礼だ」); two things set face to face are a contrast (「AのにBは……」); things matched one to one are a ratio (「学生10人に対して先生1人」). Being a verb, it has the continuative 「に対し」 and the attributive 「に対する＋noun」, both quite formal.

similar.title: 〜にとって
similar.explanation: 「にとって」 is followed by an evaluation (important, difficult, necessary) and means “from the standpoint of ...”; 「に対して」 is followed by an attitude or action directed at the other party. 「私にとって大切な人」 vs 「私に対して優しい人」.

similar.title: 〜について
similar.explanation: 「について」 marks the content being discussed or thought about; 「に対して」 marks the target of an action or feeling. 「先生について話す」 = talk about the teacher; 「先生に対して失礼だ」 = rude to the teacher.

similar.title: 〜に比べて
similar.explanation: Close to the contrast use. 「に比べて」 compares degrees: 「去年に比べて暑い」; 「のに対して」 sets two contrasting things side by side: 「兄は活発なのに対して、弟はおとなしい」.

meaning: Expresses a role, status, qualification, position, or purpose: “as ...”, “in the capacity of ...”.
connection: Noun + として／としては／としても／としての + noun

senses.label: As (a role)
senses.meaning: Doing something in a certain role, position, or capacity: “as ...”. 「としても」 means “also as ...”.
senses.connection: Noun (role / position / qualification) + として／としても
examples: As a doctor, he has saved many lives.
I came to Japan as an exchange student.

senses.label: As (a use)
senses.meaning: Something is used as or classified as something: “used as ...”, “as a ...”.
senses.connection: Noun (use / category) + として
examples: This building is used as a library.
I took up photography as a hobby.

senses.label: From the standpoint of
senses.meaning: 「としては」 makes a judgment from a certain standpoint: “as for ...”, “speaking as ...”. It can also mean “(surprisingly) for a ...”.
senses.connection: Noun + としては
examples: Personally, I agree with that opinion.
He's on the tall side for an elementary school student.

senses.label: As ... (before a noun)
senses.meaning: Before a noun, use 「としての」: “... as a ...”.
senses.connection: Noun + としての + noun
examples: I feel my responsibility as a teacher.
I think about my role as a parent.

notes: 「として」 only states status or qualification; for “to / for (someone), it's difficult / important” use 「にとって」: ✕ 「学生として、この本は難しい」 → ○ 「学生にとって、この本は難しい」.
For “better than you'd expect for ...” use 「にしては」: ✕ 「子どもとして上手だ」 → ○ 「子どもにしては上手だ」 (good for a child).
「一人として」 and 「一日として」 must be followed by a negative, meaning “not even one”: 「誰一人として来なかった」; ✕ 「誰一人として来た」.
The 「として」 in 「行こうとした」 (was about to go) and 「ほっとして」 is a different structure, not this grammar point.

etymology: Made of the case particle 「と」, which marks content or result, and 「して」, the te-form of the verb 「する」; it shares its origin with 「AをBとする」 (to treat A as B, to regard A as B). In the traditional Japanese reading of Classical Chinese texts (kanbun kundoku), 「〜として」 was often used to render expressions meaning "taking ... as" or "being ...", which gave it the sense "in the capacity of ...", and it gradually became fixed as a compound particle.
formation: 「として」 = the case particle 「と」 (specifying content) + the て form 「して」 of the verb 「する」, the same structure as 「AをBとする」 (set A as B, regard A as B). 「Aとして」 means “positioning oneself or something as A and ...” → “in the capacity of A, as A”. So what precedes is a noun of status, qualification, name or use, and what follows is what is done in that capacity; adding 「は」 gives “speaking from the position of A”, and adding 「の」 lets it modify a noun. The same “set as” logic in 「一人として〜ない」 means “not even one counted as one” → total negation.

similar.title: 〜にとって
similar.explanation: 「として」 marks status or qualification (acting as ...); 「にとって」 marks the standpoint of an evaluation (for ...). 「教師として指導する」 = guide as a teacher; 「教師にとって大切なこと」 = what matters for a teacher.

similar.title: 〜にしては
similar.explanation: 「にしては」 means “judged by that standard, the result is unexpected”: 「初めてにしては上手だ」; 「として」 only states a capacity and carries no sense of surprise.

similar.title: 〜として〜ない (一人として)
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「one + counter + として〜ない」 is total negation, “not even one ...”: 「誰一人として反対しなかった」. It must take a negative and differs from the “in the capacity of” 「として」.

meaning: Expresses purpose (“in order to ...”), cause (“because of ...”, formal), or benefit (“for the sake of ...”).
connection: Verb dictionary form / noun + の + ために; cause: plain form (often past) + ために; before a noun: ための

senses.label: In order to (purpose)
senses.meaning: Doing something deliberately to achieve a goal: “in order to ...”. The first verb is volitional, and both parts share the same subject. For non-volitional or potential verbs, use 「ように」 instead.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + ために; noun + の + ために
examples: I'm working part-time to save up for studying abroad.
I walk every day for my health.
I study every day to get into a Japanese university.

senses.label: Because of (cause)
senses.meaning: States a cause objectively: “because of ...”, “due to ...”. The cause is usually in the past or a state, and the result is usually something beyond control. Formal. Notices often write 「〜ため、」.
senses.connection: Plain form (na-adjective + な, noun + の) + ために／ため、
examples: The train was delayed because of heavy rain.
This road is closed due to construction.

senses.label: For (someone's benefit)
senses.meaning: For the benefit of someone or something: “for ...”, “for the sake of ...”. 「ためになる」 means “useful, beneficial”. Before a noun, use 「ための」.
senses.connection: Noun + の + ために／ための + noun; ためになる
examples: I make lunch boxes for my kids every morning.
This is a book for children.
This book is really worthwhile.

notes: The purpose use needs a volitional verb in the first clause, and the subjects are normally the same; with a potential form, a non-volitional verb or a negative, use 「ように」: ✕ 「日本語が話せるために勉強する」 → ○ 「話せるように勉強する」.
Purpose and reason are distinguished by form, and mixing them changes the meaning: 「休むために働く」 = work in order to rest; 「休んだために仕事が遅れた」 = because I took time off, the work fell behind.
The reason use is objective and bookish, and the second clause can't be a command or request: ✕ 「雨のために、傘を持って行きなさい」 → ○ 「雨だから、傘を持って行きなさい」.
In apologies and explanations, 「〜のため」 is more fitting than 「〜せいで」: 「電車の遅延のため、遅れてしまい申し訳ございません」; 「せいで」 would sound like shifting the blame.

etymology: ため was originally a noun that already had the meanings "benefit, advantage", "purpose", and "reason, cause" in Classical Japanese. In the traditional Japanese reading of Classical Chinese texts, 「〜のために」 was regularly used to render a Chinese preposition meaning both "for (the sake of)" and "because of", so it came to cover both purpose and cause, as it still does today.
formation: 「ために」 = the noun 「ため（為）」 + the case particle 「に」. 「ため」 means both “benefit (for the good of ...)” and “cause”, and with 「に」 (direction, arrival): acting in the direction that benefits A → “for A” (purpose, benefit); landing on A as the cause → “because of A” (reason). So when what precedes is a volitional action about to be done (dictionary form) it is purpose, and when it is something that has already happened (た form) it is reason. Since 「ため」 is a noun, nouns before it take 「の」 and it modifies nouns as 「ための」.

similar.title: 〜ように (purpose)
similar.explanation: Both express purpose. 「ために」 follows a volitional verb and the subjects are normally the same; 「ように」 follows a potential form, a non-volitional verb or a negative: 「家を買うために貯金する」 vs 「家が買えるように貯金する」.

similar.title: 〜には (purpose)
similar.explanation: 「には」 also expresses purpose, but is followed by an evaluation such as “needed, necessary, convenient, indispensable”: 「日本に留学するには、お金が必要だ」; when a concrete action follows, use 「ために」.

similar.title: 〜から (cause / reason)
similar.explanation: Close in the reason use. 「から」 is subjective and spoken, and can be followed by a command or request; 「ために」 is objective and bookish and isn't followed by commands: 「雨だから傘を持って行って」.

similar.title: 〜そのため (sentence-initial: therefore / for that reason)
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「その＋ため」 at the start of a sentence works as a conjunction meaning “therefore, for that reason”: 「電車が遅れた。そのため、会議に遅刻した」.

meaning: Acting to bring about a state or result: “so that ... can ...”, “so as not to ...”. At the end of a sentence, it expresses a wish.
connection: Verb dictionary form (non-volitional / potential verbs) / verb nai-form + ように

senses.label: So that ... can
senses.meaning: The first part is a potential or non-volitional verb, describing the state you hope to reach: “so that ... can ...”. The two parts can have different subjects. For volitional verbs, use 「ために」.
senses.connection: Potential / non-volitional verb (見える, 聞こえる, etc.) dictionary form + ように
examples: I practice every day so that I can speak Japanese well.
I wrote in large letters so that people at the back could see too.

senses.label: So as not to
senses.meaning: With the nai-form, it means taking action in advance to avoid a bad result: “so as not to ...”, “so that ... won't ...”.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + ように
examples: I'll make a note so I don't forget.
I left home early so I wouldn't miss the train.

senses.label: Wishes
senses.meaning: At the end of a sentence, 「〜ますように」 expresses a wish or blessing: “I hope ...”, “May ...”. Common on ema (shrine prayer plaques) and greeting cards.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + ますように(。)
examples: I hope I pass.
May everyone be happy.

notes: Use 「ように」 when the first clause is a potential form, a non-volitional verb or a negative, and 「ために」 when it is a volitional action you can carry out directly: ✕ 「よく見えるために前に座る」 → ○ 「よく見えるように前に座る」; ✕ 「家を買うように貯金する」 → ○ 「家を買うために貯金する」.
A bare 「〜ように。」 at the end of a sentence is an instruction in a superior's tone (「明日は遅れないように。」); saying it to a superior or client is very rude. To make a request, say 「〜ていただけますか」.
When 「ように」 is followed by 「なる」 (change) or 「する」 (effort), or preceded by 「の」 (simile), it is a different grammar point: 「話せるようになった」, 「早く寝るようにする」, 「夢のように」.

etymology: よう is written 「様」; it comes from やう, the go-on reading of the kanji 様, which later changed to よう, and originally meant "appearance, state, manner". 「〜ように」 literally means "(aiming) to become the state of ...", which gives the purpose use; the same 「様」 also gave rise to a whole family of grammar, including simile (〜のように) and change (〜ようになる).
formation: 「ように」 = the noun 「よう（様）」 (appearance, state) + the case particle 「に」 (goal, result of change). “Toward (that) state” → in order to bring about a certain state. Because 「よう」 refers to a “state”, not an “action”, what precedes is a state you can't directly carry out and can only try to realize (できる, 見える, 忘れない), which is exactly why it divides the work with 「ために」. Used alone at the end of a sentence, with 「祈る」 or 「願う」 omitted it becomes a wish (「〜ますように」), and with 「してください」 omitted it becomes an instruction (「遅れないように」).

similar.title: 〜ために
similar.explanation: Both express purpose. 「ために」 follows a volitional verb and stresses doing something deliberately to reach a goal; 「ように」 follows state-like content (potential, non-volitional, negative) and means “so that it becomes that state”: 「合格するために勉強する」 vs 「合格できるように勉強する」.

similar.title: 〜ようにする
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「ようにする」 is “try to / make a habit of”, about everyday effort: 「毎日野菜を食べるようにしている」; the purpose 「ように」 is followed by concrete actions taken to reach the goal.

similar.title: 〜ますように
similar.explanation: Same origin: the wish use at the end of a sentence, usually with 「ます」: 「合格できますように」, meaning “may ... / I hope ...”, not “in order to ...”.

title: 〜ように (purpose)

meaning: Gives an extreme example to imply that everything else goes without saying: “even ...”. 「〜さえ〜ば」 states the only condition needed: “as long as ...”.
connection: Noun (+ particle) + さえ／noun + でさえ; noun + さえ + あれば; verb masu-stem + さえ + すれば

senses.label: Even
senses.meaning: Gives an extreme example, implying everything else goes without saying: “even ...”, “not even ...”. The rest of the sentence is usually negative or surprising. After a subject, 「でさえ」 is common.
senses.connection: Noun + さえ (replaces が／を); noun + にさえ／でさえ
examples: I'm so busy I don't even have time for lunch.
At first, I couldn't even read hiragana.
Even the experts don't know the cause.

senses.label: As long as
senses.meaning: 「〜さえ〜ば」 means meeting this one condition is enough; nothing else matters: “as long as ...”, “if only ...”.
senses.connection: Noun + さえ + あれば／なければ; verb masu-stem + さえ + すれば; te-form + さえ + いれば
examples: I used to think that as long as I had money, I could do anything.
As long as you take this medicine, you'll get better soon.
As long as it's okay with you, let's go tomorrow.

notes: 「さえ」 replaces only 「が」 and 「を」; other particles must stay, or the meaning changes: 「家族にさえ言わなかった」 = didn't tell even my family; ✕ 「家族さえ言わなかった」 = even my family didn't say anything (the subject has changed).
The same 「さえ」 means “as long as” when followed by the conditional 「ば」 and “even” when not: 「水さえあれば生きられる」 = as long as there's water, we can live; 「水さえない」 = there isn't even water.
Saying 「〇〇さんでさえできる」 means “even someone like 〇〇 can do it”, implying the person is not capable, and is very rude; don't make such comparisons in front of the person or colleagues.

etymology: さえ comes from the Classical adverbial particle 「さへ」, which in the Heian period mainly meant “in addition, on top of that”. It is generally thought to derive from the verb 「添ふ（そふ）」 (to add). In older Japanese, “even” was mainly expressed by 「だに」 and 「すら」, but 「さへ」 gradually took over this use. The conditional 「〜さえ〜ば」 developed only from the early modern period on.
formation: 「さえ」 is an adverbial particle, generally thought to originally mean “add, on top of”. “Even A has been added”: you name the most unlikely, most basic example A, so the rest goes without saying → “even ...”. In the conditional 「〜さえ〜ば」, “if just A is added” is enough, reducing the necessary condition to the minimum → “as long as ...”. Since it attaches to nouns as an adverbial particle, it replaces 「が」 and 「を」, but other case particles such as 「に」 and 「で」 stay in front of it (「家族にさえ」).

similar.title: 〜さえ〜ば
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「さえ」 with the conditional 「ば」 → “as long as ...”, reducing the condition to the minimum: 「お金さえあれば」. Without 「ば」 it means “even ...”: 「お金さえない」.

similar.title: 〜すら
similar.explanation: In the sense of “even ...” the meaning is almost the same, but 「すら」 is more bookish and stronger: 「名前すら書けない」; 「すら」 generally has no conditional “as long as” use.

similar.title: 〜まで (even)
similar.explanation: 「まで」 can also mean “even”, but stresses “the range extending to an unexpected point”: 「親友にまで裏切られた」; 「さえ」 stresses “naming the most basic, minimal example”: 「挨拶さえしない」.

meaning: Adds something on top: “not only ... but also ...”. The second part often has 「も」 or 「まで」.
connection: Noun + ばかりでなく; plain form + ばかりでなく; na-adjective + な + ばかりでなく

senses.label: Not only ... but also
senses.meaning: 「AばかりでなくBも」 means not just A, but B as well: “not only ... but also ...”. B usually goes further or covers more. 「ばかりではなく」 with 「は」 sounds more formal.
senses.connection: Noun / plain form + ばかりでなく (ばかりではなく) + 〜も
examples: He speaks not only English but also Chinese.
This place is not only cheap, the food is good too.
Not only children but adults too are hooked on this anime.

senses.label: Not just ..., also ...
senses.meaning: The second part can be a command, request, or suggestion, urging someone “don't just do A, do B too”. This is where it differs from 「ばかりか」.
senses.connection: Noun + ばかりでなく／ばかりじゃなく + 〜も + なさい／てください
examples: Try reading newspapers too, not just your textbook.
Don't just study. Get some exercise once in a while too.

notes: The second part should add something in the same direction and echo with 「も」 or 「まで」: 「英語ばかりでなく、中国語も話せる」; without 「も」 the sentence feels incomplete.
Don't confuse it with 「〜てばかりいる」 (do nothing but) or 「〜たばかり」 (just did): 「遊んでばかりいる」 = does nothing but play; 「遊んだばかりだ」 = just played; 「遊ぶばかりでなく」 = not only play.
「〜ばかりでなく〜も」 can be used to advise (「遊ぶばかりでなく、勉強もしなさい」), but that is the preaching tone of an elder to a junior; don't say it to a superior or client.

etymology: ばかり is generally thought to come from 「はかり」, the noun form of the verb 「計る・量る（はかる）」 (to measure), with voicing; it originally meant "extent, approximate amount" and later became a limiting adverbial particle meaning "only, just". 「ばかりでなく」 thus means "not only (these)", expressing addition by negating a limitation.
formation: 「ばかりでなく」 = the adverbial particle 「ばかり」 (only, just) + 「で」 (continuative of the copula 「だ」) + 「なく」 (continuative of 「ない」). Literally “not only A”, and since the sentence continues through the continuative 「なく」, it naturally has to supply “what there is besides A” → “not only A but also B”. What is denied is the idea that it is “limited to A”, so the second part uses 「も」 or 「まで」 to widen the range to B. By the same logic, telling someone “don't do only A” gives the advisory use “don't just ..., also ...”.

similar.title: 〜だけでなく
similar.explanation: Same meaning. 「だけでなく」 is the most common and works in both speech and writing; 「ばかりでなく」 is slightly more bookish.

similar.title: 〜ばかりか
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「ばかりか」 is stronger, with surprise or exclamation, and the second part is often something even more extreme: 「謝らないばかりか、文句まで言う」; it also can't be used for advice or commands, whereas 「ばかりでなく」 can.

similar.title: 〜のみならず
similar.explanation: 「のみならず」 is more bookish and formal, common in speeches and writing: 「国内のみならず、海外でも人気だ」.

similar.title: 〜上に
similar.explanation: 「上に」 also adds, but stresses piling up in the same direction (good on top of good, bad on top of bad): 「安い上に、おいしい」; it is not used for advice.

meaning: A very confident conclusion based on some evidence: “must be ...”, “I'm sure ...”.
connection: Verb / i-adjective plain form + に違いない; na-adjective stem / noun + に違いない (no だ)

senses.label: Must be / surely
senses.meaning: A confident conclusion based on signs or experience: “must ...”, “surely ...”. More certain than 「だろう」 or 「かもしれない」, but still a guess. Often with 「きっと」.
senses.connection: Plain form + に違いない; noun / na-adjective stem + に違いない
examples: She practiced so hard, she's bound to pass.
The light is on, so Tanaka-san must still be home.
This must have been written by a child.

senses.label: Must have (in the past)
senses.meaning: After a past form, it guesses about a past event or someone's feelings at the time: “must have ...”. Common in novels and memories.
senses.connection: Verb / adjective ta-form + に違いない
examples: My mother must have been lonely back then.
Seeing his shocked face, I thought something must have happened.

notes: No 「だ」 after nouns or na-adjectives: ✕ 「犯人は彼だに違いない」 → ○ 「犯人は彼に違いない」; ✕ 「静かだに違いない」 → ○ 「静かに違いない」.

This is the speaker's strong subjective conviction. Asserting something about a superior or client (「部長はお疲れに違いありません」) comes across as presumptuous; to guess about them, 「お疲れではないでしょうか」 is more appropriate.
「に違いない」 means “must be”, and has nothing to do with “no difference”; to say “there is no difference” use 「違わない」 or 「同じだ」.

daily.example: He must have overslept again.

daily.example: This handwriting has to be my sister's.

work.example: I'm sure the client will love this proposal.

etymology: 「違い（ちがい）」 is the nominalized continuative form of the verb 「違う」, meaning "error, difference". 「に違いない」 literally means "there is no mistake (on this point)", i.e. "it is certainly so". The more formal written 「に相違ない」 has exactly the same structure.
formation: 「に違いない」 = the case particle 「に」 (in respect of ...) + the noun 「違い」 (mistake, difference) + 「ない」. Literally “there is no mistake on the point of A” → “it must be A”. It vouches for the judgment “A” itself, so the content of the judgment is placed directly in front, and after nouns and na-adjectives the copula 「だ」 is not added. It expresses the speaker's inner conviction and doesn't need rigorous grounds, so it is often used for confident inferences based on signs or intuition.

similar.title: 〜はずだ
similar.explanation: 「はずだ」 is “should be”, reckoned from reasoning or facts; 「に違いない」 is the speaker's strong conviction based on evidence or intuition. 「8時に出たから、もう着いたはずだ」 vs 「あの顔は、何かあったに違いない」.

similar.title: 〜に決まっている
similar.explanation: 「に決まっている」 is more colloquial and more dogmatic, often carrying a subjective assertion or emotion: 「そんなの嘘に決まってる」; 「に違いない」 is slightly more bookish, used in writing and narration.

similar.title: 〜かもしれない
similar.explanation: Both are conjectures, but the degree of certainty differs: 「かもしれない」 is “maybe”, with a possibility of around half or even less; 「に違いない」 is “must be”, almost certain.

meaning: Strongly rules out a possibility based on logic, facts, or common sense: “there's no way ...”, “can't possibly ...”.
connection: Verb / i-adjective plain form + はずがない; na-adjective + な + はずがない; noun + の + はずがない

senses.label: Can't possibly
senses.meaning: Concludes from logic, facts, or common sense that something is impossible: “there's no way ...”, “can't be ...”. It is a stronger denial than 「ないはずだ」 (shouldn't be). 「はずはない」 adds emphasis.
senses.connection: Plain form + はずがない／はずはない (polite: はずがありません)
examples: There's no way someone so kind would say something that cruel.
I locked it, so the door can't be open.
He practices every day. There's no way he'll lose.

senses.label: No way! (disbelief)
senses.meaning: 「そんなはずはない」 strongly rejects what someone said or what you're seeing, expressing surprise and disbelief. In speech, 「が」 can be dropped: 「はずない」.
senses.connection: そんな + はずはない／はずがない／はずない
examples: That can't be! I'm sure I put it right here.
What, he's not coming? No way.

notes: 「はずがない」 (can't possibly) and 「ないはずだ」 (shouldn't) differ in strength: 「彼が知らないはずだ」 is only an inference, while 「彼が知っているはずがない」 is a strong denial.
「こんなはずじゃなかった」 means “it shouldn't have turned out like this (but it did)”, expressing regret or surprise, which is different from “impossible”.
Answering a client or superior directly with 「そんなはずはありません」 amounts to saying “you're wrong”, which is harsh; better to say 「確認いたしますので、少々お待ちください」.
Nouns need 「の」: ✕ 「彼が犯人はずがない」 → ○ 「彼が犯人のはずがない」.

daily.title: Defending a friend
daily.description: Strongly denying a false rumor about a friend.
daily.example: There's no way he'd lie.

daily.title: When something's missing
daily.description: Disbelief when something you put away has vanished.
daily.example: That can't be. It was right here a minute ago.

daily.title: Joking about your cooking
daily.description: Joking that a first attempt can't possibly taste good.
daily.example: There's no way the first dish I ever made is going to taste good.

work.title: Checking data

work.example: Everything has been inspected, so there is no possibility of defective items getting mixed in.

etymology: はず is written 「筈」 and originally referred to the notch at the end of an arrow that fits onto the bowstring (矢筈). The notch and the string necessarily fit together, which extended to "it stands to reason, naturally so". 「はずがない」 thus means "there's no reason for that", i.e. it's simply impossible.
formation: 「はずがない」 = the noun 「はず（筈）」 (the reasoning by which things ought to be so) + 「が」 + 「ない」. The notch of an arrow and the bowstring are meant to fit together, so 「はず」 means “by reason it must be so”; 「はずがない」 means “such a reason doesn't exist” → by the facts and common sense, it's simply impossible. Because what is denied is the “possibility in reason”, it is far stronger than 「〜ないだろう」 and is often used to rebut or express disbelief (「まさか、そんなはずがない」). Replacing 「が」 with 「は」 gives 「はずはない」, with contrastive emphasis. 「はず」 is a noun, so nouns before it take 「の」 and na-adjectives take 「な」.

similar.title: 〜わけがない
similar.explanation: Almost the same meaning, both “impossible”. 「わけがない」 is more colloquial and subjective, often emotional; 「はずがない」 leans toward “judging it impossible from facts and reason”.

similar.title: 〜はずだ
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「はずだ」 is “by reason it should be ...”, 「はずがない」 is “by reason it can't be ...”; 「ないはずだ」 is only “should not be”, much weaker than 「はずがない」.

similar.title: 〜まい
similar.explanation: 「まい」 also expresses negative conjecture, “probably won't”, but is more bookish and weaker: 「彼はもう来るまい」; 「はずがない」 is a strong denial with grounds.

meaning: Having a certain quality or tendency: “-ish”, “-like”, “prone to ...”. In casual speech it can also mean “seems like”.
connection: Noun / i-adjective stem + っぽい; verb masu-stem + っぽい; (casual) plain form + っぽい

senses.label: -ish / -like
senses.meaning: After a noun, it means having a certain quality or feel: “-ish”, “-like”. Often negative, suggesting something isn't as it should be, as in 「子どもっぽい」 (childish) and 「安っぽい」 (cheap-looking).
senses.connection: Noun / i-adjective stem + っぽい (子どもっぽい, 安っぽい, 男っぽい, etc.)
examples: He's already 30, but he keeps saying such childish things.
This bag looks a bit cheap.

senses.label: Color or texture
senses.meaning: A neutral description of a color or texture close to something: “-ish”. For example, 「白っぽい」, 「黒っぽい」, 「水っぽい」.
senses.connection: Color noun / noun + っぽい (白っぽい, 黒っぽい, 水っぽい, etc.)
examples: That whitish building is the station.
This soup is a little watery.

senses.label: Prone to
senses.meaning: After a verb masu-stem, it describes a personality trait: “tends to ...”, “quick to ...”. For example, 「忘れっぽい」, 「怒りっぽい」, 「飽きっぽい」.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + っぽい (忘れっぽい, 怒りっぽい, 飽きっぽい, etc.)
examples: I've gotten forgetful lately.
My dad has a short temper, so be careful.

senses.label: Seems like (casual)
senses.meaning: In young people's casual speech, it follows a noun or sentence to make a guess: “seems like ...”, “looks like ...”. Very casual; avoid it in formal settings.
senses.connection: Noun / plain form + っぽい
examples: Looks like that shop is closed today.
It looks like rain tomorrow.

notes: 「〜っぽい」 often carries a casual or negative evaluation: 「子どもっぽい」 = childish, 「安っぽい」 = cheap-looking. Using it to evaluate a person or a client's belongings to their face is rude.
「らしい」 is “true to type, with the typical traits”, 「っぽい」 is “not really so but looks like it”: 「男らしい」 = manly (a compliment); calling a woman 「男っぽい」 may offend her.
The conjectural 「〜っぽい」 (「風邪っぽい」「雨っぽい」) is very casual, so don't use it in work reports: ✕ 「明日は雨っぽいです」 → ○ 「明日は雨のようです」.
Attachment to verb ます stems is limited to a few fixed expressions (忘れっぽい, 怒りっぽい, 飽きっぽい); you can't coin new ones freely: ✕ 「食べっぽい」.

daily.title: Talking about a friend's personality
daily.description: Friends chatting about someone's immature behavior.
daily.example: That guy gets so childish whenever he's angry.

daily.title: Describing a color to a clerk
daily.description: Explaining roughly what color you want.

daily.description: Making fun of your own poor memory.
daily.example: I've been so forgetful lately. I keep losing my keys.

work.title: Chatting with coworkers vs. reporting to your boss
work.description: 「っぽい」 is very casual and only suits chats with close coworkers. With a boss or client, say 「〜ようです」.
work.example: Looks like Tanaka-san is off today.

etymology: 「っぽい」 is an adjective-forming suffix, generally thought to have formed by adding a geminate consonant before 「ぽい」; early examples include 「荒っぽい」, 「俗っぽい」, and 「水っぽい」. Its exact origin is disputed. In recent decades its range has kept expanding, and it can now attach freely to all kinds of nouns and even whole clauses, which is regarded as a colloquial, newer usage. (Compare English "-ish", which has similarly spread to casual uses like "sixish" or "I'm done-ish".)
formation: 「っぽい」 is a suffix that forms adjectives, meaning “having a touch or air of ...”. Attached to the stem of a noun or adjective, the whole becomes a new i-adjective: “contains an element of A” → “is A-ish, has the feel of A” (「子どもっぽい」「白っぽい」); attached to the ます stem of a few verbs, “contains an element of that action” → “apt to ...” (「忘れっぽい」). Because it only says “has an element of”, not “is”, it often means “not really so but looks like it”, and in speech it has developed a vague conjecture, “seems to be ...”. Being an i-adjective, it conjugates as 「っぽく・っぽかった・っぽさ」.

similar.title: 〜らしい (typical / true to type)
similar.explanation: 「らしい」 means “true to its name, having the typical traits of that kind of thing”, mostly positive: 「学生らしい服装」; 「っぽい」 means “not really that, but with that feel”, often a casual or negative evaluation: 「子どもっぽい」 = childish.

similar.title: 〜ようだ・〜みたいだ
similar.explanation: Close in the conjecture use. 「ようだ」 and 「みたいだ」 are the ordinary forms of conjecture; 「っぽい」 is very casual speech and isn't used in formal settings: 「風邪っぽい」 → 「風邪のようだ」.

similar.title: 〜気味
similar.explanation: 「気味」 means “slightly tending toward ...”, mostly for unwelcome physical conditions or states: 「疲れ気味」「風邪気味」; 「っぽい」 has a wider range and can also describe personality, color and texture.

similar.title: 〜がち
similar.explanation: 「がち」 means “apt to ... (often)”, mostly for undesirable things: 「忘れがち」 describes the frequency of the behavior; 「忘れっぽい」 describes a person's character (forgetful).

meaning: Checks something you can't quite remember, with someone else or yourself: “What was ... again?”. Also used to reminisce: “We used to ..., didn't we?”.
connection: Plain form (noun / na-adjective + だ／だった) + っけ; verb ta-form + っけ; polite: でしたっけ／ましたっけ

senses.label: What was it again?
senses.meaning: You knew it but can't recall it right now, so you check with someone or yourself: “... again?”. Said with a questioning tone, and can combine with 「ね」 or 「な」. 「でしたっけ」 works with a boss, but it still sounds a bit casual.
senses.connection: Noun / na-adjective + だっけ／だったっけ／でしたっけ; verb + たっけ／ましたっけ
examples: Hmm, what day is it today again?
Tanaka-san is from Osaka, right?
What time did the last meeting start again?

senses.label: Reminiscing
senses.meaning: Talking to yourself about the past, with nostalgia: “we used to ..., didn't we”. Often with 「よく」 or 「昔は」.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + っけ(な)
examples: As a kid, I used to swim in this river a lot.
I used to go fishing with my dad a lot, didn't I?

notes: 「っけ」 is used with people you know to confirm something you “used to know but can't recall”; with a superior or client it sounds forgetful and not serious; even 「でしたっけ」 is casual, and in formal settings say 「〜でしたでしょうか」 or 「念のため確認させてください」.
It can't be used to ask for new information you never knew: ✕ (asking a passerby) 「駅はどこだっけ？」 → ○ 「駅はどこですか」.
Attachment: for nouns and na-adjectives in the present, add 「だ」; for verbs use the た form or 「んだっけ」: ✕ 「明日は何曜日っけ」 → ○ 「何曜日だっけ」; ✕ 「何時に行くっけ」 → ○ 「何時に行くんだっけ」.

daily.description: A name slips your mind while chatting with a friend.
daily.example: What was that guy's name again?

daily.title: Checking a meeting time
daily.description: Confirming when you're meeting a friend.
daily.example: What time are we meeting tomorrow again?

daily.title: Looking at old photos
daily.description: Seeing old photos and remembering the past.
daily.example: We used to play together in this park a lot, didn't we?

work.title: Checking the schedule with a coworker
work.description: Use 「でしたっけ」 to check with a close coworker or boss.
work.example: Our next meeting is Thursday, right?

work.title: Checking a deadline with your boss informally
work.description: 「でしたっけ」 works with a boss but sounds casual. With clients or in formal settings, use 「〜でしょうか」.
work.example: The deadline was the end of this month, wasn't it?

etymology: It is generally thought to come from the Classical Japanese auxiliary 「けり」, which expressed recollection and exclamation. けり was later simplified to 「け」, and in colloquial speech a geminate was added to give 「っけ」. It kept the sense of "recalling the past" and further developed the use of checking a memory with the listener.
formation: 「っけ」 is formed from the assertive or completive 「だ」 or 「た」 plus the final particle 「っけ」. 「っけ」 is generally thought to come from the old retrospective auxiliary 「けり」, which originally meant “recalling it now, so it was ...”, so it inherently points to “a past or memory already known”. After 「だ」 or 「た」 it means “(I remember it's) ... , wasn't it?”: said to the listener, it asks them to confirm your memory; said to yourself, it is recalling the past. Because it is about “retrieving an existing memory”, it can't be used to ask for new information you never knew.

similar.title: 〜たものだ (recollection)
similar.explanation: Close in the recollection use. 「たものだ」 looks back with feeling on things that happened repeatedly in the past and can be used in writing: 「昔はよくここで遊んだものだ」; 「っけ」 is casual spoken recollection: 「よくここで遊んだっけ」.

similar.title: 〜かな
similar.explanation: Both can be said to yourself. 「かな」 asks yourself about something you don't know or aren't sure of: 「明日は雨かな」; 「っけ」 confirms something you “used to know but can't recall”: 「明日は何曜日だっけ」.

similar.title: 〜じゃない（か）(confirmation)
similar.explanation: Both are used to confirm. 「じゃない（か）」 is when you're fairly sure and ask the other to agree: 「これ、君のじゃない？」; 「っけ」 is when your memory is hazy and you ask the other to remind you.

meaning: Using the chance of doing one thing to do another as well: “while you're at it”, “on the way”.
connection: Verb dictionary form / ta-form + ついでに; noun + の + ついでに; (adverb) ついでに

senses.label: While going to do ...
senses.meaning: After the dictionary form, it means doing something extra while going to do the main task: “while you're ...ing, also ...”. The first part is the main purpose; the second is the extra.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + ついでに
examples: When you go to the post office, could you mail this letter too?
Since you're going to the convenience store, could you grab me some milk?

senses.label: Since I was already ...
senses.meaning: After the ta-form, it means since you've already done something (or come somewhere), you take the chance to do something else: “while I was there, I also ...”.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + ついでに
examples: While I was in Tokyo, I met up with an old friend.
While I was on a business trip to Osaka, I also stopped by Kyoto.

senses.label: On the way (noun)
senses.meaning: After an action noun, add 「の」: “while on a ...”. For example, 「散歩のついでに」 and 「出張のついでに」.
senses.connection: Noun + の + ついでに
examples: I picked up some bread while I was out for a walk.
While I was shopping, I stopped by the bank.

senses.label: While you're at it (adverb)
senses.meaning: On its own at the start of a sentence, it works as an adverb: “while I was at it”, “also”. Often used to add a request or extra point.
senses.connection: ついでに、+ sentence
examples: I cleaned your room too while I was at it.
While you're at it, could you copy this document as well?

notes: Put the main purpose in the first clause and the incidental action in the second; reversing them changes the meaning: 「買い物のついでに銀行に寄る」 = shopping is the main thing, stopping by the bank on the side; 「銀行のついでに買い物する」 = the bank is the main thing.
When visiting a client, 「近くに来たついでに寄りました」 sounds as if the other party is only a casual stop on the way, showing little regard; say 「近くまで参りましたので、ご挨拶に伺いました」.
「ついでに」 doesn't mean two actions at the same time: ✕ 「歩くついでに話す」 → ○ 「歩きながら話す」.

etymology: 「ついで」 is written 「序で」. It comes from 「つぎ」, the continuative form of the verb 「次ぐ（つぐ）」 (to follow, to come next), plus 「て」, which became 「ついで」 through i-onbin. It originally meant "order, sequence", and extended to "an incidental opportunity, convenience". The kanji 「序」 itself also means "order".
formation: 「ついでに」 = the noun 「ついで（序で）」 (order, an opportunity that follows) + the case particle 「に」. 「ついで」 comes from 「次ぐ」, “follow, come right after”, so 「Aのついでに」 means “following A, taking the occasion of A” to do B on the side. This structure makes A the main business and B an extra “hitching a ride”, and the roles can't be swapped. What precedes can be a verb (dictionary form = on the way of doing A, た form = after doing A) or 「noun＋の」; used alone with no preceding clause it is the adverb “while at it”.

similar.title: 〜がてら
similar.explanation: 「がてら」 is more bookish and follows action nouns such as 「散歩」 or 「買い物」 or the ます stem, meaning “while doing ..., also ...”: 「散歩がてら、パンを買いに行く」; 「ついでに」 is more colloquial and attaches more freely.

similar.title: 〜を兼ねて
similar.explanation: 「を兼ねて」 means one thing serves two purposes at once: 「趣味と実益を兼ねて」; 「ついでに」 means doing another thing on the side of the main one, with a clear main and secondary.

meaning: Do something while a state still lasts: “while ...”. Or something changes gradually during a process without you noticing.
connection: Verb dictionary form / ている-form / nai-form / i-adjective + うちに; na-adjective + な + うちに; noun + の + うちに

senses.label: While it lasts
senses.meaning: The first part is a state that will end or change. You do something while it lasts, because later it will be harder: “while ...”. The second part is usually a deliberate action.
senses.connection: i-adjective / na-adjective + な / noun + の + うちに (若いうちに, 今のうちに, etc.)
examples: Please eat it while it's hot.
You should travel to lots of countries while you're young.
Let's get our homework done now while we can.

senses.label: Before ... happens
senses.meaning: 「ないうちに」 means hurrying to do something before an unwelcome situation arises: “before ...”. It feels more urgent than 「前に」.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + ないうちに
examples: Let's hurry home before it starts raining.
Let's go home before it gets dark.

senses.label: Before you know it
senses.meaning: While an action continues, a change happens naturally: “as I kept ..., I ended up ...”. The first part is usually 「〜ている」, and the second is an involuntary change.
senses.connection: Verb ている-form + うちに
examples: As I kept watching Japanese dramas, my Japanese got better.
I fell asleep while reading a book.

senses.label: As long as
senses.meaning: 「うちは」 means “while this state lasts (it's fine)”, implying things will be different once it ends.
senses.connection: i-adjective / na-adjective + な + うちは
examples: While you're young, you can do anything.
As long as I'm healthy, I want to keep working.

notes: 「〜ないうちに」 means “before it ...”, not “when it doesn't ...”: 「暗くならないうちに帰ろう」 = let's go home before it gets dark.
In the “while” use, the second clause is something the speaker actively does, with the urgency of “it'll be too late afterward”; for a plain time order or habitual sequence use 「前に」: 「寝る前に歯を磨く」.
In the “before you know it” use, the second clause is a change that happens naturally and can't be a volitional act of your own: 「話しているうちに眠くなった」; ✕ 「話しているうちに電話をかけた」 → ○ 「話している間に電話がかかってきた」.
For a fixed period with a clear start and end, use 「間に」: 「夏休みの間に宿題を終わらせる」.

etymology: うち is written 「内」, originally meaning "inside, interior"; it is the same word as 「うち（家・内）」 meaning "home". Applied to time, it means "within a certain time span", giving the use "during ... (while it lasts)"; and since a change happens in the middle of an ongoing process, it further developed the "without noticing" use.
formation: 「うちに」 = the noun 「うち（内）」 (inside, within a range) + the case particle 「に」 (time, range). A span of time is seen as a “circle”, and doing something inside it → “during ...”. The circle is drawn by the preceding state (若い, 明るい, 温かい), and when the state ends the circle disappears, hence the sense “hurry and do it while it's still ...”; 「ないうちに」 is “within the circle of ‘not yet ...’”. If a person stays inside the circle and something changes by itself, you get “before you know it”.

similar.title: 〜間・〜間に
similar.explanation: 「間に」 means something happens at a point within a clearly defined period, with no urgency: 「留守の間に泥棒が入った」; 「うちに」 carries the nuance “now's the time, it'll be too late afterward”: 「若いうちに旅行しよう」.

similar.title: 〜まえに
similar.explanation: 「ないうちに」 and 「前に」 can both be translated as “before ...”. 「前に」 just gives the time order: 「寝る前に歯を磨く」; 「ないうちに」 carries the urgency of “hurry before it's no longer ...”: 「冷めないうちに食べて」.

similar.title: 〜か〜ないかのうちに
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「〜か〜ないかのうちに」 means “no sooner than ...”, with the two events almost simultaneous: 「ベルが鳴るか鳴らないかのうちに、教室を飛び出した」.

meaning: The cause of a good result, with gratitude: “thanks to ...”. Used ironically with bad results.
connection: Plain form + おかげで; na-adjective + な + おかげで; noun + の + おかげで (sentence-final: おかげだ)

senses.label: Thanks to
senses.meaning: The cause of a good result, with thanks to it: “thanks to ...”.
senses.connection: Plain form / noun + の + おかげで
examples: Thanks to my teacher, I passed the JLPT.
Thanks to the medicine, my fever went down.

senses.label: It's all thanks to
senses.meaning: At the end of a sentence, 「〜のおかげだ／です」 gives credit for a good result. Often in the pattern 「〜のは〜のおかげです」.
senses.connection: 〜のは + noun + の / plain form + おかげだ／おかげです
examples: I was able to pass because of all your help.
It's thanks to my family that I've come this far.

senses.label: Greeting: thanks for asking
senses.meaning: 「おかげさまで」 is a set greeting used when answering someone's question about how you are, even if they didn't actually help.
senses.connection: おかげさまで、+ news
examples: I'm doing well, thank you.
“How's work?” “Going smoothly, thanks.”

senses.label: Ironic: all because of
senses.meaning: With a bad result, it sounds sarcastic or blaming: “thanks a lot, ...”, “it's all because of ...”. Mostly between people who know each other well.
senses.connection: Plain form / noun + の + おかげで + bad result
examples: Thanks to you being late, we missed the train.
Thanks to your fooling around, we got yelled at by the teacher.

notes: Used for a bad result it is sarcastic: 「あなたのおかげで遅刻したよ」 = thanks to you I was late (it's your fault). It is harsh to say to someone; use 「おかげで」 to thank only for good results.
When asked how you are, it is customary to say 「おかげさまで、元気にしております」 even if the other person didn't directly help; just answering 「はい、元気です」 isn't wrong, but lacks the polite expression of thanks.
Using 「おかげ」 about yourself (「私のおかげで成功した」) sounds boastful and is unpopular in Japan; crediting others is appropriate: 「皆さんのおかげで成功しました」.
Nouns need 「の」: ✕ 「先生おかげで」 → ○ 「先生のおかげで」.

etymology: 「おかげ」 is written 「御陰・御蔭」, made of the honorific prefix 「お（御）」 + 「陰・蔭（かげ）」 (shade), originally referring to the sheltering protection of gods and buddhas, later extended to favors and help given by others. 「おかげさまで」 thus means "thanks to (you and the gods)". The お蔭参り pilgrimages to Ise Shrine, popular in the Edo period, also reflect this religious origin.
formation: 「おかげで」 = the honorific prefix 「お」 + the noun 「かげ（陰・蔭）」 (shade, shelter) + the causal 「で」. 「かげ」 originally means the protection of gods, buddhas or other people, and 「お」 adds respect, so 「Aのおかげで」 means “thanks to A's protection (this result came about)”. Its essence is therefore “receiving a favor, expressing gratitude”, so it is used for good results; 「おかげだ」 at the end of a sentence credits A. Used for bad results, it deliberately turns the “favor” upside down, which makes it sarcasm. The greeting 「おかげさまで」 follows the same logic: crediting your well-being to the other person and those around you.

similar.title: 〜せいで
similar.explanation: Also a cause, but with a different evaluation: 「おかげで」 is for good results and carries thanks; 「せいで」 is for bad results and carries blame. 「雨のおかげで涼しい」 vs 「雨のせいで中止になった」.

similar.title: 〜ために
similar.explanation: Close in the cause use. 「ため」 is a neutral, objective cause with no thanks or blame, used mostly in writing and notices: 「台風のため、休校になった」.

similar.title: 〜から (cause / reason)
similar.explanation: 「から」 is the most ordinary way to give a reason, with no evaluation, and can be followed by a request or command; 「おかげで」 only states the source of the result and expresses gratitude.

meaning: The cause of, or blame for, a bad result: “because of ...”, “it's ...'s fault”. 「せいか」 suggests an uncertain cause.
connection: Plain form + せいで; na-adjective + な + せいで; noun + の + せいで (sentence-final: せいだ)

senses.label: Because of (blame)
senses.meaning: The cause of a bad result, with a tone of complaint or blame: “because of ...”, “thanks to ...”.
senses.connection: Plain form / noun + の + せいで
examples: The game was canceled because of the rain.
I stayed up late playing games, so I couldn't get up in the morning.

senses.label: It's ...'s fault
senses.meaning: At the end of a sentence, 「〜のせいだ／です」 says who is to blame. Often in the pattern 「〜のは〜のせいだ」. Also used to admit your own fault.
senses.connection: 〜のは + noun + の / plain form + せいだ／せいです
examples: It's my fault we lost.
The failure was due to a lack of preparation.

senses.label: Maybe because
senses.meaning: 「せいか」 is the speaker's vague guess about a cause: “maybe because ...”. The result isn't necessarily bad.
senses.connection: Plain form / noun + の + せいか
examples: Maybe it's my age, but I get tired easily these days.
Maybe it's lack of sleep, but I have a headache.

senses.label: Blaming
senses.meaning: 「〜のせいにする」 means putting the blame on someone or something else: “blame ... for it”.
senses.connection: Noun + の + せいにする
examples: You shouldn't blame others for your own mistakes.
Stop blaming everyone else for everything.

notes: 「せいで」 carries blame, and saying 「あなたのせいで」 to someone's face is an accusation that hurts; when explaining causes at work, use neutral 「〜のため」 or 「〜により」: ✕ 「システムのせいで遅れました」 → ○ 「システム障害のため、遅れが生じました」.
For good results use 「おかげで」; with 「せいで」 the meaning becomes “it's all because of ...”: ✕ 「先生のせいで合格できた」 → ○ 「先生のおかげで合格できた」.
Describing your own mistake with 「〜のせいで」 looks like shifting responsibility; 「人のせいにする」 means “to blame others”, which is poorly regarded in Japanese workplaces.

etymology: 「せい」 is traditionally written with two kanji meaning roughly "what is done". One theory traces it to the Sino-Japanese word しょい ("that which someone has done"), whose reading changed to せい; it originally meant "what (someone) did, the result they caused", and extended to "reason, cause, blame". Because opinions on its origin differ, it is mostly written in kana today.
formation: 「せいで」 = the noun 「せい（所為）」 (a result produced by someone's doing → responsibility) + the causal 「で」. “Because A caused it” → the result is attributed to A; since 「せい」 itself carries a sense of “responsibility”, the result is mostly bad, which naturally gives a blaming tone. With the question particle 「か」 it becomes 「せいか」, “perhaps because of A”, with an uncertain cause; 「Aのせいにする」 “sets” the responsibility as A's → to blame A.

similar.title: 〜おかげで
similar.explanation: Also a cause, but with the opposite evaluation: 「せいで」 is for bad results and carries blame, 「おかげで」 is for good results and carries thanks. 「雨のせいで中止になった」 vs 「雨のおかげで涼しくなった」.

similar.title: 〜せいか
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「せいか」 means “perhaps because of ...”, with an uncertain cause and a weaker tone, usable for good or bad results: 「年のせいか、疲れやすい」.

similar.title: 〜ために
similar.explanation: Close in the cause use. 「ため」 is a neutral, objective cause, suited to reports and notices: 「事故のため、電車が遅れた」; 「せいで」 carries blame and is avoided in formal settings.

meaning: Evaluates something from a person's or organization's standpoint: “for ...”, “to ...”.
connection: Noun + にとって／にとっては／にとっても／にとっての + noun

senses.label: For / to
senses.meaning: A judgment from a person's or organization's point of view: “for ...”, “to ...”. The second part is usually an evaluation like 「大切だ・難しい・ありがたい・問題だ」, not a specific action.
senses.connection: Noun (person / organization) + にとって
examples: To me, this photo is a treasure.
Finding an apartment is tough for international students.

senses.label: For ..., though / also
senses.meaning: 「にとっては」 adds contrast: “for ..., on the other hand”. 「にとっても」 means “for ... as well”.
senses.connection: Noun + にとっては／にとっても
examples: It may be easy for adults, but it's hard for children.
This decision is a big issue for the company as well.

senses.label: For ... (before a noun)
senses.meaning: Before a noun, use 「にとっての」: “... for ...”.
senses.connection: Noun + にとっての + noun
examples: What does happiness mean for a child?
My most precious treasure is my family.

notes: It is followed by an evaluation or judgment (大切だ, 難しい, 必要だ), not by an attitude or action toward a person: ✕ 「先生にとって親切だ」 → ○ 「先生に対して親切だ」.
「にとって」 doesn't express status: ✕ 「教師にとって、学生を指導する」 → ○ 「教師として、学生を指導する」.
Saying 「部長にとっては簡単でしょう」 to a boss amounts to judging a superior's ability, which is considered rude in Japan; to learn their view, just ask 「部長はどうお考えですか」.

etymology: Made of the case particle 「に」, marking the target, and 「取って」, the te-form of the verb 「取る」 (to take); the old form 「に取りて」 became 「にとって」 through a geminate sound change. Literally "taking it with regard to ...", i.e. "viewed from the standpoint of ...". It is now fully grammaticalized and almost always written in kana.
formation: 「にとって」 = the case particle 「に」 (object, standpoint) + the て form 「とって」 of the verb 「取る」 (take). Literally “take it into A's hands and look at it” → “weigh it from A's standpoint” → “for A”. Since it weighs the meaning and value for A, it is followed by an evaluative predicate (大切だ, 難しい, ありがたい, 必要だ) and not by actions done to A. Adding 「は」 gives contrast (「私にとっては」 = for me, at least), and adding 「の」 modifies a noun (「私にとっての幸せ」).

similar.title: 〜にしたら・〜にすれば
similar.explanation: 「にしたら／にすれば」 means “putting yourself in someone's position”, mostly to guess another person's feelings: 「親にしたら心配だろう」; 「にとって」 is the general “for ...” evaluation.

similar.title: 〜として
similar.explanation: 「として」 marks status or qualification: 「教師として働く」; 「にとって」 marks the standpoint of an evaluation: 「教師にとって大切なこと」.

similar.title: 〜に対して
similar.explanation: 「に対して」 is followed by an attitude or action directed at the other party: 「子どもに対して厳しい」; 「にとって」 is followed by an evaluation: 「子どもにとって難しい」.

similar.title: 〜から見ると・〜からすると
similar.explanation: 「から見ると」 means “judging by observing from ...”, stressing viewpoint and opinion: 「外国人から見ると不思議だ」; 「にとって」 stresses “what it means or is worth to someone”.
